newsitem.title: UK: Clinton, Yeltsin face off for tough summit on NATO.
newsitem.headline: Clinton, Yeltsin face off for tough summit on NATO.

text.p: By Nicholas Doughty, Diplomatic Correspondent
Facing their toughest summit so far, U.S. President Bill Clinton and Russian President Boris Yeltsin will try to resolve growing tensions over NATO enlargement when they meet in Helsinki this week.

Success, even if limited, could pave the way for improved security across Europe in the 21st century. Failure could carry a heavy cost as NATO prepares to invite a handful of countries from the former Soviet bloc to join the alliance.

Yeltsin, on fighting form after months of illness, attacked NATO's plans to take in new members as a "blockade" on Monday and demanded that Russia be seen as an equal if a return to Cold War tensions was to be avoided.
"There has not been such a difficult meeting as this between me and an American president," he said.
Yeltsin, who will be meeting Clinton for the 11th time, must be careful not to appear weak in front of his communist and nationalist critics at home.
But Clinton, too, has said he also expects the summit on Thursday and Friday to be tough and U.S. officials have begun to play down any expectation of a breakthrough.
"I'm not sure there will be an agreement," U.S. Defence Secretary William Cohen told reporters on Monday, saying he sensed that Russia recognised NATO enlargement was bound to go ahead.
Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov met Clinton in Washington on Monday and said afterwards Moscow would not change its opposition to NATO enlargement.
"There will likely continue to be some disagreements after the summit in Helsinki," said White House spokesman Mike McCurry. "I can't imagine that we will solve all the issues..."

The summit was delayed by one day after Clinton had to undergo surgery following a knee injury last week. Yeltsin, for so long the focus of health concerns, has made fun of the fact that Clinton will be either in a wheelchair or on crutches.
Nevertheless, the two men have established a good working relationship at previous summits. Helsinki will be their first meeting since they both won re-election last year.

The United States is hoping that it can persuade Russia to accept, however grudgingly, that NATO enlargement will not present a threat to its security and that it can work -- as a major, well-respected power -- with an expanded alliance.
Time is running out since NATO leaders will invite several countries to start membership talks at a July summit in Madrid. Those are widely expected to be Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic.
Yeltsin wants legally binding commitments in the NATO relationship, including guarantees that allied troops and nuclear arms will not be deployed in new member states.
NATO is offering Russia a new relationship through a special charter, which would give Moscow the right to consultation on European security issues but no power to veto the alliance's plans.

But the United States and its allies reject the Russian push for more binding commitments and Yeltsin's other demand -- that former Soviet republics, particularly the Baltic states, should be barred forever from NATO membership.
There are also problems with arms control, which is intimately linked with the NATO issue and with Russia's perception that it is surrounded by potential enemies.

The North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) has offered to make major changes to a 1990 treaty on conventional forces in Europe, to meet Russian concerns about a Western arms buildup close to its borders.

Clinton is expected to discuss this and the deadlock over nuclear arms. The 1993 START-2 strategic arms pact, which provides for major cuts in the U.S. and Russian arsenals, has not come into force because the Russian Duma (parliament) views it as damaging to the country's security.
U.S. officials have spoken of preparing for a possible new agreement that would go for even deeper cuts, but insist that the Duma must ratify START-2 first.

On the economic front, Yeltsin has complained bitterly that Russia is left out of key international groupings. Having given reformers the lead in a cabinet reshuffle this week, the Kremlin chief is expected to press that view hard in Helsinki.

Washington supports an increased Russian role in the Group of Seven (G7) leading industrialised nations and may back its efforts to join other groupings like the World Trade Organisation and the Paris Club, which deals with debt.
Clinton may also offer more cash to help Russia fight corruption and strengthen reforms.
But whether the package on offer will be enough to convince Yeltsin that he has won the best possible deal in the face of NATO enlargement remains to be seen.
